clue.text: Part of house that’s left frequently

blocks.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left
an old or poetic word for often

explanation.surface: A room in the house that people keep walking out of.
explanation.definitionFit: The roof space at the top of a home, reached by ladder and used for storage, is one of its rooms.

clue.text: The first thirteen characters in charge of certain weapons

blocks.note: the first thirteen letters of the alphabet run from A to M, written A TO M
IC is the usual abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: The opening members of a cast are put in command of some weaponry.
explanation.walkthrough: The characters are letters, not people: the first thirteen of the alphabet go from A to M.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuclear bombs and missiles are described with this adjective, so it means pertaining to one particular kind of arms.

clue.text: Dog escape initially unreported in China

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter only of the word it follows
in places what comes before it inside the word that follows

blocks.note: on the lam means on the run, so a lam is an escape
the first letter of unreported
rhyming slang: china plate means mate, a friend

explanation.surface: A dog's escape went unreported in China at first.
explanation.walkthrough: China here is Cockney rhyming slang (china plate = mate), not the country.
explanation.definitionFit: A malamute is a large Alaskan sled breed, a powerful working canine related to the husky.

clue.text: Fools English judge with appeal in drugs case

indicators.note: in puts the preceding letters inside the word that follows
a case holds things, so the drugs act as an outer wrapper

blocks.note: E is ecstasy, so drugs in the plural are Es
E is the abbreviation for English
J is the abbreviation for judge
it means sex appeal, as in the it girl

explanation.surface: An English judge hearing an appeal in a drugs trial calls the defendants idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: Eejit is an Irish and Scottish spelling of idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: Eejit is the Irish and Scots colloquial form of idiot, so the plural means silly people or dolts.

clue.text: Duly pick at random in this?

definitions.text: Duly pick at random in this?

indicators.note: something done at random has no set order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A fairground game in which you properly choose without looking.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the anagram and the definition: you pick at random from a lucky dip.
explanation.definitionFit: A lucky dip is a barrel of wrapped prizes into which you reach and pull one out blindly, so you choose by chance.

clue.text: Learnt about something seen in natural history programme

definitions.text: something seen in natural history programme

indicators.note: about can mean around or turned round, so the letters are moved about

blocks.note: the six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone picked up a fact from watching a wildlife documentary.
explanation.definitionFit: A stag's branched horn is the sort of thing a wildlife film on deer shows; the definition is a loose example.

clue.text: Somehow getting us to use oranges is extravagance

indicators.note: somehow says the result comes by some unspecified rearrangement

blocks.note: all fourteen letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Persuading us to cook with oranges is a wild excess.
explanation.definitionFit: Outrageousness is the quality of going beyond reasonable limits, which is what extravagance means in its sense of excess.

clue.text: Firm stem

blocks.note: first meaning: loyal and steadfast, an adjective
second meaning: to stop a flow, as of blood from a wound, a verb

explanation.walkthrough: Stem looks like a plant's stalk but is the verb for checking a flow; the answer is also spelt stanch in that sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A staunch supporter is steadfast and loyal, and to staunch bleeding is to stop it flowing.

clue.text: Balloon modelling at a store

indicators.note: modelling means shaping, so the letters are moulded into a new form

blocks.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is fashioning balloon animals in a shop.
explanation.definitionFit: An aerostat is any lighter-than-air craft such as an airship or blimp, and a hot-air or gas balloon is one.

clue.text: I am getting cooking vessel covered in titanium, and other things in the kitchen

indicators.note: covered in means wrapped by, so the chemical symbol goes round what precedes it

blocks.note: contracted as I'm
a pan for frying or boiling
Ti is the chemical symbol for titanium

explanation.surface: A titanium-coated pan sits among the other kitchen utensils.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen is orchestral slang for the percussion section, not a room for cooking.
explanation.definitionFit: Kettledrums belong to the percussion section, which players nickname the kitchen, alongside cymbals and other noisemakers.

clue.text: Child scandal finally admitted some time back somewhere in Ireland

indicators.note: finally picks just the closing letter of the word before it
something admitted is let inside, so it goes within the first word
back means the period word is read from right to left

blocks.note: a kid is a child
the last letter of scandal
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A child-abuse scandal from years ago was finally admitted to in an Irish town.
explanation.definitionFit: Kildare is a county and town in the Irish province of Leinster, west of Dublin, so it is a place in that country.

clue.text: Mistakes made by early riser at parcel service

blocks.note: a cockerel crows at dawn, so it rises early
UPS is United Parcel Service, a courier company

explanation.surface: Errors made by a keen early-morning worker at a delivery firm.
explanation.walkthrough: Cock-up is British slang for a blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A cock-up is informal British slang for a botched job or blunder, so the plural means errors.

clue.text: Bums showing in bed, which is most indelicate

indicators.note: showing in means visible inside, so one word is placed within the other

blocks.note: British slang for backsides
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: Bare bottoms visible in bed is about as rude as it gets.
explanation.walkthrough: Arse is the British spelling of ass.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse means crude or vulgar, so its superlative names whatever is crudest and least refined in manners.

clue.text: Running aground somewhere in Mexico

indicators.note: running suggests a rush that leaves things disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A ship has run onto the shore off a Mexican coast.
explanation.walkthrough: Durango is inland, so the shipwreck picture is a false scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Durango is a state in northern Mexico and also its capital city, so it names a place there.

clue.text: Bowler might be discarded so on the smallest provocation

annotation.answer: AT THE DROP OF A HAT

blocks.note: surface reading: a cricketer could be dropped from the team in some way
setter's reading: a bowler is a type of headwear, and letting it fall describes the phrase

explanation.surface: A cricket bowler might be dropped for the slightest reason.
explanation.walkthrough: Bowler looks like the cricketer, but it is the hard round felt hat; the straight definition follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means instantly and without needing any reason, from the signal once given by letting headgear fall.

clue.text: Letter from Greece about mostly cheerless dramatic scene

indicators.note: mostly means all but the final letter is kept
about means going round, so the Greek letter surrounds the other word

blocks.note: tau is the Greek letter T
bleak means dreary and cheerless

explanation.surface: A Greek letter about a gloomy theatrical moment.
explanation.walkthrough: The shortened word goes inside the Greek letter after its second letter, not around the whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A tableau is a striking group of figures, often motionless on stage, so it is a theatrical picture.

clue.text: Lost aria about a Spanish girl

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so these letters are moved around

blocks.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A forgotten operatic song concerning a young woman from Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosalita is a Spanish female given name, a pet form of Rosa, so it names a girl from that country.

clue.text: A meaningful number getting first couple of parts of well-known song from No, No, Nanette confused in audition

indicators.note: confused means mixed up, here swapping whole words rather than letters
an audition is a hearing, so the result is judged by its sound

blocks.clueFragment: first couple of parts of well-known song from No, No, Nanette
blocks.note: the song is Tea for Two; its first two words swapped round are spoken this way

blocks.clueFragment: well-known song from No, No, Nanette
blocks.note: the last word of the same song title

explanation.surface: A significant figure arises when a famous showtune's opening gets muddled when heard.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap Tea and for in Tea for Two and you say 'for tea two', which is how forty-two is said. In The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy 42 is the answer to life, the universe and everything.
explanation.definitionFit: In Douglas Adams's comic novel this figure is the ultimate answer, so it is the number with the most significance.

clue.text: Bribes ordinary seamen in vessels

indicators.note: in places the seamen inside the vessels word

blocks.note: O is an abbreviation for ordinary
the Royal Navy, Britain's sailors
submarines are vessels

explanation.surface: Sailors aboard ships are being paid off.
explanation.walkthrough: Ordinary seamen invites OS, but here ordinary and seamen are taken separately.
explanation.definitionFit: To suborn is to induce someone, often by payment, to commit perjury or another wrong, so it means to buy off.

clue.text: University official siting sportsground on top of hill

blocks.note: short for recreation ground, a British public playing field
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A college administrator decides to put a playing field on a hilltop.
explanation.walkthrough: On top of works because this is a down clue: the first piece sits above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: At Scottish and some European universities the rector is an elected senior officer, so the title names an academic head.

clue.text: Communist teams hidden in trading centre

indicators.note: hidden in means tucked inside, so the teams go within the market word

blocks.note: a team of eleven is an XI in Roman numerals, so teams are XIs
a mart is a market

explanation.surface: Teams of comrades are concealed in a marketplace.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden in looks like a hidden-word signal but here XIS goes inside MA...RT.
explanation.definitionFit: Followers of Karl Marx's doctrines are communists, so the two words name the same political adherent.

clue.text: Note avian creature that’s brought up a bit of foliage?

indicators.note: in a down clue brought up means read upwards, from bottom to top

blocks.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale
a creature that flies is a bird

explanation.surface: Take note of a bird that has carried up a leaf in its beak.
explanation.definitionFit: The midrib is the central vein running down a leaf, so it is a part of a plant's leafy growth.

clue.text: American doctor put in prison

blocks.note: first meaning: a junior hospital doctor in the US
second meaning: to confine, especially in wartime

explanation.surface: A US physician is jailed.
explanation.definitionFit: In US hospitals a newly qualified medic in training is so called, and as a verb it means to detain or confine.

clue.text: Mimeograph, for example, clients ordered

indicators.note: ordered means put into a new sequence, so the letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Customers have requested a copying machine.
explanation.walkthrough: Ordered looks like customers placing an order, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A mimeograph prints copies through a waxed sheet cut with the design, so it is a kind of printing template device.

clue.text: Sun always having awful darts coverage

indicators.note: awful means very bad, so the letters are in a mess and need rearranging
coverage means wrapping round, so the rearranged letters cover the other word

blocks.note: the five letters to be rearranged around the other piece
ay or aye is an old word for ever, always

explanation.surface: A tabloid paper always has terrible darts reporting.
explanation.walkthrough: Sun looks like the British tabloid newspaper, whose sports pages might cover darts; here it is the star in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Daystar is a poetic name for our star, the one that rules the daytime sky, and also for the morning star.

clue.text: Excellent American drama school

blocks.note: rad is slang for excellent, short for radical
A is an abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: A first-rate acting academy in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: RADA is the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London, so American misleads.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Academy of Dramatic Art is a famous London institution training actors, known by its initials.

clue.text: If sold out, worth getting reordered from another planet?

indicators.note: reordered means put in a different sequence, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: all fourteen letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sell-out show is worth having its order changed.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase usually means superb; the question mark flags that it is read literally as alien.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally, something beyond our world comes from elsewhere in space, as an alien would.
